title: Get them to behave with no skills whatsoever: Part 3 The Language You Use Date Published: June 3, 2026
author: Dominic Salles
summary: This is Part 3 in Salles's practical series on classroom behaviour, providing a toolbox of specific phrases and questions that any teacher can use immediately, regardless of charisma, relationship-building skill, or emotional self-regulation. The article is explicitly not a self-improvement guide — it does not ask teachers to become better people, become trauma-informed, or build deep relationships first — but instead provides a laminated set of tools that produce behavioural improvement from the first day. Salles organises the language into four phases: psychological safety framing (before students start), managing task performance and memory (redirecting during work), eliciting and upgrading thought (after initial responses), and feedback and redirection. The psychological safety language reframes mistakes as the expected and desired state: 'I'm not expecting anyone to get this right first time. That's how we learn' — removing the shame that makes students refuse to engage. The elicitation phase includes high-leverage sequences such as 'Yes, and...' and 'Who can say this even better?' that invite elaboration without threatening the initial respondent. Salles acknowledges the artificiality of some techniques (like tracking the speaker) but explains that what makes students genuinely listen is knowing their opinions matter and that they don't have to agree with the teacher.
points: The article's core claim is that effective classroom language is a skill-independent toolbox: an Early Career Teacher can use these phrases tomorrow and produce measurable improvement without years of experience, emotional maturity, or charisma.

Psychological safety language works best when it precedes the task rather than repairing damage after failure — phrases like 'I'm testing you on this before I teach it, because your brain will want to correct all the mistakes' reframe the cognitive task itself rather than just managing anxiety.

The 'Show me your best thinking' sequence is designed to decouple cognitive effort from the shame of wrong answers — when students know the teacher wants to see their thinking rather than the right answer, the fear of exposure drops sufficiently to allow genuine engagement.

Salles's Phase 3 elicitation phrases ('Yes, and...' / 'Who can say this even better?' / 'In your pairs, argue the opposite of that') function to keep the intellectual work in the room rather than concentrating it in the teacher — they are conversation-structuring moves, not just niceness.

The standing technique for extreme 'I don't know' situations is a high-stakes last resort: asking a student to stand until they have a thought and then immediately affirming whatever they offer — it may feel artificial but normalises the expectation that all students will eventually contribute.
quotes: Everything I'll show you, an ECT could do tomorrow, with instant impact. You don't have to watch your emotions, and be the adult in the room. You don't have to go out of your way to build great relationships.

'I'm testing you on this before I teach it, because your brain will want to correct all the mistakes. That's just how the brain works.' / 'I'm not expecting anyone to get this right first time. That's how we learn.' / 'No one learns anything without making mistakes. I'm looking for useful mistakes.'
'Show me your best thinking.' / 'I know you don't know the answer. Show me your best thinking. Then I can work out how to help you get even better.'

It feels very artificial and controlling to tell students to track the speaker, and it is the most difficult routine for teachers to establish. What makes students listen is knowing not just that they could be next, but that their opinion is actually valued.
'I've noticed you were successful when...' / 'Thank you for... I need you to' / 'I've noticed that... I need you to'

This might feel a little extra, but it really works. Ask that student to stand. Tell them as soon as they have an idea they can sit down. (As soon as they sit down, you hear their idea and quickly offer your approval — it may genuinely have been a big deal for this student).
